hero.name: Rohan
hero.who: a 19-year-old physics student in Ranchi who believes toppers are simply born gifted

story.h: The cousin who has it all
story.b: Rohan's cousin Vivek has just cracked a top engineering entrance, and the whole family in Ranchi is celebrating with rasgullas. At the party, an aunty pats Rohan's shoulder and says some children are simply born brilliant. Rohan nods. He has believed this for years. Vivek was always the gifted one, and Rohan, now in the second year of BSc Physics at a local college, was the ordinary one. On the bus back to Lalpur, he decides there is no point trying to compete with people like Vivek. He deletes the coding course he had saved on his phone. Talent, he thinks, is something you either get at birth or you do not.

ask.q: Rohan gives up because he thinks his cousin was born brilliant. What is wrong with his thinking?
o: Nothing, since some people are simply gifted from birth
He should work twice as hard just to prove the aunty wrong
He is ignoring the hidden support, timing and practice behind Vivek's success
ask.why: Calling it pure talent hides everything else that went into Vivek's result. Working twice as hard out of hurt pride misses the lesson too. Once Rohan sees the support, timing and practice behind success, he can stop comparing birth gifts and look at what he can actually build.

chapters.take: Talent explains less than we think. Look at what was hidden behind it.

story.b: A week later, Rohan drops off sweets at Vivek's house in Harmu and sees his cousin's room properly for the first time. A desk by the window, a good lamp, shelves of guidebooks, fast internet. Vivek mentions two years of coaching in Kota, an uncle who checked his maths every Sunday, and a mother who handled everything else so he could study. Vivek says, without any showing off, that he could not have done it alone. Rohan thinks of his own home, a room shared with two younger brothers, evenings spent helping at his father's mobile repair shop. Vivek is clever and worked hard. But he also had a great deal of help. On the way out, his friend Shalini messages him, upset about her results.

ask.q: Shalini says she must be less clever than the classmate who topped. What could Rohan point out?
o: That the topper may also have had help, like coaching and a quiet room, that she did not
That she should accept she is not the topper type
That the topper was just lucky and did no real work
ask.why: Nobody succeeds alone. The topper probably worked hard and also had hidden advantages, like coaching, time and a quiet room. Saying Shalini is not the type ignores those, and calling it pure luck dismisses real effort. Seeing the full picture is fairer to both of them.

chapters.take: Behind every success story is help you cannot see from outside.

story.b: In October, Rohan asks a question in physics class that makes Professor Tirkey pause and smile. The next day she asks him to help set up the lab for the first-year practicals. It is a small thing, two hours a week. But in those hours he handles equipment the others only see in exams. He asks more questions, and she starts lending him books. By December she suggests his name for a summer project at a research centre. Rohan sees how one small break led to more attention, more practice and another chance. That evening at home, his younger brother Sonu, in Class 6, is in tears over fractions. Rohan almost leaves him to it, thinking he will catch up later.

ask.q: Sonu is a little behind in Class 6 maths. When is the best time for Rohan to help?
o: In Class 10, when the marks really count
Now, since a small early boost can grow into a big lead
Never, since the school will notice and handle it
ask.why: Small early advantages snowball. A child who gets a little ahead now gains confidence, attention and practice, which pulls him further ahead. Waiting for Class 10 lets the gap grow instead, and a crowded class may never notice. Early help is the cheapest help.

chapters.take: Small early advantages grow, and so does help given early.

story.b: Rohan reinstalls the coding course on his phone. But he has no laptop, and the computer at his father's shop is used for billing. So he asks the college lab assistant if he can use a machine from four to six every evening. The assistant agrees, as long as Rohan switches off the fans when he leaves. Those two hours become his. He writes small programs: a marks calculator, a tool for his father to track repair orders. Most of them break. After six weeks his code is still clumsy, and a classmate glances at his screen and laughs. He says real coders are born, not made. Rohan walks home past Ranchi Lake that evening, thinking about those six weeks.

ask.q: After six weeks of evening practice, Rohan's code is still clumsy. What should he do?
o: Keep his daily practice slot, since real skill takes years of steady work
Switch to a skill that seems to come more naturally
Watch tutorial videos instead of writing code
ask.why: Deep skill takes a very long time of focused practice, and six weeks is only the start. Switching skills just restarts the clock, and watching videos feels productive but builds little. Keeping his regular slot gives Rohan the hours that real mastery needs.

chapters.take: Mastery is slow. Protect a regular practice slot and let the hours pile up.

story.b: In May, Rohan starts his summer project at the research centre outside the city. He grew up in a home where you do not question elders. You listen, you nod, you touch their feet at festivals. It is a habit he loves. But on the third day, he notices that a senior researcher, Dr. Minz, has used the wrong unit in a calculation. If nobody says anything, a whole week of readings will be off. Rohan's stomach tightens. Every instinct from home tells him it is not his place. He looks at his notebook again, then at the senior's door, then at his own hands. The others in the lab are busy and have not noticed.

ask.q: Questioning a senior feels wrong to Rohan, but the error will spoil a week of work. What should he do?
o: Stay quiet, since juniors should not question seniors
Point it out loudly in the group meeting to show he is sharp
Politely raise it with Dr. Minz in private, showing his working
ask.why: Respect for elders is a good habit, but here silence would waste a week of readings. Making a show of it in a meeting could embarrass the senior. Raising it politely and privately, with his working, keeps the respect and protects the work.

chapters.take: Know the habits you grew up with, and choose when they help you.

story.b: That summer, something shifts in Lalpur market. Shopkeepers who never touched a computer want customers to order on WhatsApp and pay by UPI. The sweet shop owner asks Rohan's father if anyone can make a simple order list. The tailor next door wants reminders sent when clothes are ready. Rohan realises he is in an odd, lucky spot. He has just enough coding to help, he knows every shopkeeper by name, and the need is brand new. A year earlier nobody wanted this. A few years later, big apps might do it all. He thinks about how timing helped Vivek too, in its own way. He also thinks he is nowhere near an expert yet.

ask.q: Local shops suddenly want simple order systems, and Rohan knows only basic coding. What should he do?
o: Wait until he is an expert before offering anything
Offer to help a few shops now, while the need is fresh
Leave it to big companies, since small towns rarely get chances
ask.why: Timing opens doors that do not stay open forever. Waiting to become an expert may mean the chance has gone. Assuming small towns get no chances shuts the door himself. Helping a few shops now lets Rohan learn and earn while the need is new.

chapters.take: Notice the chances your moment offers, and be kind to those who missed theirs.

story.b: Rohan is in his final year now. He still uses the college lab from four to six, though he has bought a second-hand laptop with money from his first eight shop clients. The sweet shop's order list crashed twice in the first month, and he fixed it both times. Professor Tirkey has written him a recommendation for a master's programme. Sonu, now in Class 7, explains fractions to his friends with a smug face. Rohan no longer thinks of Vivek as born gifted. He thinks of him as someone who worked hard and had a lot of help, which is a far more useful idea. When a junior says he is just not a natural, Rohan tells him about the free lab hours.

chapters.take: Success is effort plus help, time and timing. Much of that can be built or shared.
